sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: Community acquired Pneumonia (CAP) is defined as an acute infection of the pulmonary parenchyma that is acquired outside a hospital or healthcare setting[cite: 709]. It typically presents with symptoms of acute infection, accompanied by the presence of an acute infiltrate on a chest radiograph or auscultatory findings (such as altered breath sounds and/or localized rales)[cite: 710]. To diagnose CAP, at least one systemic feature (either a symptom complex of sweating, fevers, shivers, aches and pains and/or temperature of 38°C or more) must be present, with no alternative explanation for the illness[cite: 711]. Community acquired pneumonia remains a disease with high mortality if not recognized timely and correctly managed[cite: 712].

sections.heading: Purpose
sections.body: To provide accurate and update information to care providers who manage CAP cases in the hospital so that diagnosis and appropriate management of CAP are done timely and correctly[cite: 714].

sections.heading: Aim
sections.body: To improve outcome of patients presenting at King Faisal Hospital with community acquired pneumonia[cite: 716].

sections.heading: Rationale
sections.body: Failure to diagnose CAP timely or administering the wrong antibiotics, can have serious and potentially fatal consequences[cite: 718]. This guideline provides recommendations to prevent delay or incorrect treatment, aiming to reduce hospital stay and minimize complications from pneumonia[cite: 719].

sections.heading: Scope of Guideline
sections.body: This guideline is intended for all healthcare provides managing adult or adolescent patients with community-acquired pneumonia[cite: 721]. This can be in the general outpatient department, internal medicine departments and Accident & Emergency department[cite: 722]. The guideline applies to all adult or adolescent patients presenting with CAP that are seen in King Faisal Hospital, both inpatients and outpatients[cite: 723].

sections.heading: Competencies Required
sections.body: Every medical doctor working in the mentioned areas where patients with CAP are managed has access to the guidelines and is competent to apply them[cite: 725].

sections.heading: Definition of Key Terms
bullets: CAP: Community Acquired Pneumonia [cite: 728]
COPD: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease [cite: 729]
CURB-65: scoring system used to assess the severity of pneumonia based on 5 criteria: confusion, urea, respiratory rate, blood pressure, and age [cite: 730]
HIV: Human Immunodeficiency Virus [cite: 731]
ICU: Intensive Care Unit [cite: 732]
MRSA: Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus [cite: 733]
PSI Score: Pneumonia Severity Index Score [cite: 734]
PO: per os [cite: 735]
IV: intravenous [cite: 736]
OD: once daily [cite: 737]
BID: bis in die, twice a day [cite: 738]
TDS: ter die sumendum, three times a day [cite: 739]
QID: quater in die, four times a day [cite: 740]

sections.heading: Assessment of Patients - Patient History
bullets: Symptoms of an acute lower respiratory tract illness: cough, sputum production, shortness of breath, chest pain[cite: 744].
Systemic signs: fevers, shivering, sweating[cite: 745].

Co-morbidities: COPD, Asthma, Diabetes Mellitus, Chronic Kidney Disease, Congestive Heart Failure, Coronary Artery disease, malignancy, asplenia, chronic neurological diseases and chronic liver diseases[cite: 746].
Smoking and alcohol abuse[cite: 747].
HIV status[cite: 748].
Recent (last 3 months) antibiotic use[cite: 749].
Recent hospitalization (last 3 months)[cite: 750].
Tuberculosis infection / treatment in the past[cite: 751].

sections.heading: Assessment of Patients - Physical Examination
bullets: Vital signs: Respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, temperature, blood pressure, heart rate[cite: 753].
Inspection, palpation, percussion and auscultation of chest[cite: 754].

sections.heading: Assessment of Patients - Etiology
sections.body: Organisms commonly associated with pneumonia are listed below[cite: 756].
bullets: Bacterial pathogens: Streptococcus pneumonia, Moraxella catarrhalis, Staphyloccus aureus, Haemophilus influenza, Chlamydia pneumoniae, Group A Streptococci, Enterobacterales[cite: 757, 758].
Atypical non-zoonotic bacterial pathogens: Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Legionella spp., Chlamydia pneumoniae[cite: 759].
Atypical zoonotic bacterial pathogens: Chlamydophila psittaci (psittacosis), Coxiella burnettii (Q fever)[cite: 760].
Bronchiectasis or CF: Pseudomonas aeruginosa[cite: 761].
Mycobacterium tuberculosis can also present as CAP[cite: 762].
Viral pathogens: Influenza, SARS-CoV-2, other coronaviruses, rhinoviruses, parainfluenza viruses, adenoviruses, respiratory syncytial virus, human metapneumovirus[cite: 763, 765].
Pathogens related to CAP in immunocompromised patients are Burkholderia, fungi, P. jirovecii, Nocardia species[cite: 766].

sections.heading: Assessment of Patients - Diagnostics
bullets: Chest X-ray (CXR) is recommended as primary radiographic imaging[cite: 769]. Expected findings include lobar consolidation, cavitary lesions, and interstitial pattern[cite: 770, 771, 772, 773]. In cases with high suspicion and inconclusive CXR, an additional chest CT is suggested[cite: 774]. Compare with previous images if available[cite: 774].
Full blood count[cite: 775].
C-reactive protein[cite: 776].
Procalcitonin in patients who need admission[cite: 777].
Urea, creatinine and electrolytes as part of severity assessment[cite: 778].
Arterial blood gasses in patients with severe pneumonia[cite: 779].
COVID-19 rapid diagnostic test or PCR when findings are suggestive of viral pneumonia[cite: 780].
Blood culture (2 bottles for adults) in patients who need admission[cite: 781].

Sputum culture can be valuable in certain settings, including in hospitalized patients with severe symptoms, and when patients have a history of MRSA, Pseudomonas or Enterobacterales[cite: 782]. It is not recommended as a routine investigation for CAP in the outpatient setting[cite: 783].
HIV screening in severe pneumonia patients[cite: 784].

In cases of severe pneumonia, rapid tests for Streptococcus pneumoniae and Legionella, along with respiratory virus panel PCR tests (including influenza), can be requested based on their availability[cite: 785].

sections.heading: Decision to Hospitalise Patients
sections.body: Not all patients with pneumonia require hospital admission. A risk-assessment should be performed for all patients with CAP to decide which patient can safely be managed at home[cite: 788]. Main decision is based on severity of the disease. Other important considerations are the patient's socio-economic status and home circumstances[cite: 789].

sections.heading: Severity of Illness Assessment - Overview
sections.body: A number of severity of illness assessment tools have been developed to assist clinicians in assessing the severity of community-acquired pneumonia[cite: 791]. Assessment of the severity of infection is important since it will determine appropriate site of care, microbiological work-up and empiric antibiotic treatment[cite: 792]. The Infectious Disease Society of America (IDSA) recommended in 2019 using the PSI score over CURB-65 score to determine which patient can be safely treated as an outpatient[cite: 793].

sections.heading: Severity of Illness Assessment - PSI Score Risk Classes
bullets: Patients with CAP and scores of <50 (class 1) and 51-70 (class 2) are thought to be mild and potentially suitable for management at home[cite: 800].
Patients with scores of 71-90 (class 3) are considered moderately ill and need to be observed in hospital initially[cite: 801].
Patients with scores of > 91 (class 4 & 5) are thought to be severely ill, and need consideration for admission to a high-care or even intensive care unit[cite: 802].

sections.heading: Severity of Illness Assessment - Other Scores
bullets: Other scores, such as CURB-65, are less accurate, but could be used because of its simplicity and do not require the measurement of the urea level[cite: 804].

None of the scoring systems replace clinical assessment. Important additional factors, such as socioeconomic deprivation and co-morbidity, must influence the decision on hospitalization and treatment[cite: 805].
The PES score was developed in 2015 to predict the microbiological etiology of CAP caused by PES pathogens[cite: 808, 809].
Patients are at risk for MRSA, multidrug-resistant Enterobacteriaceae and Pseudomonas if: Hospitalization AND IV antibiotics in the last 90 days, or PES score ≥ 5[cite: 810, 811, 812].

sections.heading: Severity of Illness Assessment - ICU Admission Criteria
sections.body: In addition to the tables mentioned above, the ATS/IDSA also give recommendations on identifying patients who should be admitted to ICU for intensive monitoring and treatment[cite: 816]. Patients requiring ICU-level care are:
bullets: Patients with hypotension requiring vasopressors or respiratory failure needing mechanical ventilation[cite: 818].
Patients with three or more of the following (minor) criteria, of course assessed on individual base[cite: 819]:
Blood urea nitrogen ≥ 20 mg per dL (7.14 mmol per L)[cite: 820].
Confusion or disorientation[cite: 821].
Core temperature < 36°C[cite: 822].
Hypotension requiring aggressive fluid resuscitation[cite: 823].
Multilobar infiltrates[cite: 824].
Partial pressure of oxygen/fraction of inspired oxygen ratio ≤ 250[cite: 825].
Platelet count < 100,000 per µL (100x10^9 per L)[cite: 826].
Respiratory rate ≥ 30 breaths per minute[cite: 827].
White blood cell count < 4,000 per µL (4.00x10^9 per L) due to infection alone (i.e., not chemotherapy induced)[cite: 828].

sections.heading: Therapy and Follow-up - Supportive Therapy
bullets: Patient is given explanation about the diagnosis, prognosis and the therapy he/she will receive[cite: 831].
Analgesics and rehydration are started when indicated[cite: 832].
Oxygen therapy: up to 5L/min via nasal cannula; 6-10L/min via simple non face mask; more than 10L/min via non-rebreathing face mask or high-flow nasal cannula[cite: 833, 834].

sections.heading: Empirical Antibiotic Therapy - Outpatients
bullets: Treatment options for previously healthy outpatients; no antibiotic use in past 3 months: Amoxicillin 1 gm PO every 8 hours for 5-7 days OR Amoxicillin-clavulanic acid 625 mg po every 8 hours or 1 gram PO every 12 hours for 5-7 days OR Doxycycline 100mg PO every 12 hours for 7 days PLUS: Azithromycin 500 mg PO daily for 3 days[cite: 837, 838, 839, 841, 842].

Outpatients with comorbidities or antibiotic use in past three months: Amoxicillin-clavulanate 1 g PO BID for 5-7 days + Azithromycin 500 mg PO once daily for 3 days OR Third generation cephalosporin (such as cefixim 400 mg PO daily or 200 mg PO BID) for 5-7 days + Azithromycin 500 mg PO once daily for 3 days OR Amoxicillin-clavulanate 1 g PO BID + Clarithromycin 500 mg PO BID for 5-7 days[cite: 844, 845, 846, 847].

Penicillin allergy: Doxycycline 100 mg PO every 12 hours for 7 days OR Levofloxacin* 750 mg PO OD (5 days) or moxifloxacin* 400 mg PO OD (5-7 days) (*Note: Fluoroquinolones should be avoided in patients with suspected TB)[cite: 848, 850, 851, 852].
If previous colonization with MRSA or Pseudomonas or high risk for multidrug-resistant organisms: empirically cover and total treatment will be 7-14 days[cite: 853].

sections.heading: Empirical Antibiotic Therapy - Inpatients
bullets: Beta-lactam antibiotics as intravenous ceftriaxone or amoxicillin-clavulanic acid for 5-7 days PLUS azithromycin 500 mg oral daily for 3-5 days[cite: 855, 856].
In case of penicillin allergy: cephalosporins or respiratory fluoroquinolones (levofloxacin) are options[cite: 857].

In patients with severe pneumonia who have a history of prior antibiotic exposure, piperacillin-tazobactam is occasionally chosen as the initial treatment[cite: 858]. This decision is always made in consultation with an infectious diseases specialist or pulmonologist[cite: 859].

Previous colonization with MRSA or pseudomonas in previous year OR high risk based on PES-score: MRSA: 3rd generation cephalosporin (7 days) + vancomycin + macrolide[cite: 860, 861]. Pseudomonas: Piperacillin-tazobactam / cefepime (7-14 days) + macrolide[cite: 861]. Enterobacteriaceae: piperacillin-tazobactam / cefepime (7-10 days) + macrolide[cite: 861].
The American Thoracic Society (ATS)/Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) guidelines recommended that patients with CAP should be treated for a minimum of five days[cite: 862].

Before stopping therapy, the patient should be afebrile for 48 to 72 hours, breathing without supplemental oxygen (unless required for pre-existing disease), and have no more than one clinical instability factor (defined as heart rate >100 beats/minute, respiratory rate >24 breaths/minute, and SBP ≤90 mmHg)[cite: 864, 865].

sections.heading: Therapy and Follow-up - Special Considerations
bullets: Aspiration pneumonia. The 2019 American Thoracic Society (ATS) and Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) guidelines on CAP and the 2023 ERS/ESICM/ESCMID/ALAT guidelines for the management of severe community-acquired pneumonia guidelines recommend against routinely adding anaerobic coverage for patients with (suspected) aspiration pneumonia[cite: 866].
Corticosteroids are not recommended as adjunctive therapy for treatment of non-severe CAP[cite: 867].

However, given the potential beneficial effect on length of hospital stay and 28-day mortality, the use of corticosteroids is now recommended in patients with severe CAP who meet one of the following criteria: mechanical ventilation with PEEP > 5 cm water; high-flow oxygen with a FiO2 > 50% and PaO2:FiO2 ratio < 300; nonrebreathing mask with PaO2: FiO2 ratio < 300; PSI class V and the absence of relative contraindication (e.g. history suggesting aspiration, pneumonia caused by influenza)[cite: 868, 869, 870].

sections.heading: Patients' follow-up and complications
bullets: Clinical response is expected within 48 hours otherwise there is a need to reconsider the therapy[cite: 872].
Shifting from IV to oral takes place when patients improve and can take oral therapy[cite: 873].
Complications are to be looked for and managed (empyema, meningitis, septicemia, shock)[cite: 874].

After hospital discharge, routine use of follow-up chest imaging in adults with CAP who are improving after the start of antibiotic treatment is not recommended, unless there are complications[cite: 875].
Patients at high risk of lung cancer should benefit from a chest CT scan 4-8 weeks after discharge[cite: 876].
